claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries cause local stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The local stress concentrations caused by pile-ups promote microcracking and catastrophic damage during straining.
Cryogenic rolling followed by annealing is an applicable thermomechanical treatment for a lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Rolling should be performed below approximately -100 degrees Celsius and followed by annealing near 500 degrees Celsius for a short duration.
Cryogenic rolling followed by annealing will refine the dual-phase lamellar architecture.
The treatment will reduce lamellar spacing.
The treatment will produce a more homogeneous distribution of misorientations and recovered regions at internal boundaries.
Cryogenic rolling introduces a high density of dislocations uniformly across the lamellar colonies.
The subsequent annealing partially relaxes and recrystallizes the deformed regions.
The combined treatment minimizes sharp internal-boundary contrasts that lead to dislocation pile-ups.
Reducing pile-ups will diminish local stress concentrations and delay microcrack initiation during straining.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will maintain or increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The effectiveness of the treatment depends on control of deformation temperature, strain rate, and annealing time.
The exact magnitudes of the strength and ductility improvements are uncertain and may depend on processing and initial microstructure.
